summary.text: Blood vessels are the tubular structures of the circulatory system that transport blood in animal bodies.
They carry blood cells, nutrients and oxygen to most of the body's tissues, and they carry waste products and carbon dioxide away from them.
There are five types of blood vessel: arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins.

facts.label: Capillary job
facts.value: Where water and chemicals are exchanged between blood and tissues

facts.label: Tissues without them
facts.value: Cartilage, epithelium, and the lens and cornea of the eye

facts.label: Vein valves
facts.value: Prevent backflow of blood pumped against gravity

facts.label: Capillary length
facts.value: 9,000 to 19,000 kilometres in human muscles, by later studies

items.prompt: Blood leaves the heart with every heartbeat. Which vessels carry it away from the heart?
items.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry blood from the capillaries back towards it.

items.prompt: Water and chemicals pass between the blood and the tissue around it. In which vessels does that exchange take place?
items.explain: Capillaries are the vessels where the exchange of water and chemicals between blood and tissues occurs.

items.prompt: A student is puzzled that the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood. What explains it?

options.label: Artery walls remove oxygen from the blood
Vessels are named by direction relative to the heart, not by oxygen content
That artery is really a vein that was mislabeled
Only in the lungs do arteries carry oxygen-poor blood by chance

items.explain: Vessels are grouped as arterial or venous by whether blood flows away from or toward the heart. The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs to be oxygenated.

items.prompt: Blood in the leg veins is pushed upward by surrounding muscles, against gravity. What stops it from sinking back down?

options.label: Wave-like squeezing of the vein walls
A thick outer layer that holds blood in place

items.explain: Veins can have valves that prevent backflow of blood pumped against gravity by surrounding muscles. Vessels do not move blood by peristalsis.

items.prompt: A blockage cuts off one path, yet nearby tissue still gets blood because vessels link up to offer alternative routes. What is such a connection called?
items.explain: When vessels connect to form a region of diffuse vascular supply, it is called an anastomosis, and it provides alternative routes for blood if there is a blockage.

items.prompt: What propels blood through the arteries and arterioles?

options.label: Wave-like squeezing of the artery walls

items.explain: Blood is propelled through arteries and arterioles by pressure generated by the heartbeat; vessels have no appreciable peristalsis.

paragraphs.heading: The body's tubing
paragraphs.text: Blood vessels are the tubes of a circulatory system that carry blood through an animal's body. They bring blood cells, nutrients and oxygen to most tissues, and they carry waste products and carbon dioxide away. A few tissues have no blood vessels at all and are called avascular; examples are cartilage, epithelium, and the eye's lens and cornea.

paragraphs.heading: Five kinds of vessel
paragraphs.text: There are five types of blood vessel. Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The others are the arterioles; the capillaries, where water and chemicals pass between the blood and the tissues; the venules; and the veins, which bring blood from the capillaries back toward the heart. The word vascular, used for anything about blood vessels, comes from the Latin vas, meaning vessel, while capillary comes from a Latin word for hair.

paragraphs.heading: Arterial and venous
paragraphs.text: Vessels are roughly grouped as arterial or venous, depending on whether their blood flows away from the heart or toward it. In general, arteries and arterioles carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the body, and veins and venules carry oxygen-poor blood back to the lungs. The lungs flip this: the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood to them, and the pulmonary vein brings oxygen-rich blood back. In all other arteries hemoglobin is 95–100% loaded with oxygen, while in all other veins it is about 75%.

paragraphs.heading: Layers of the wall
paragraphs.text: The inner layer of a vessel wall, the tunica intima, is the thinnest: a single layer of flat cells over a thin layer of connective tissue. The middle layer, the tunica media, is thickest in arteries and can be rich in smooth muscle, which controls how wide the vessel is. The outer layer, the tunica adventitia, is made entirely of connective tissue and is the thickest layer in veins. Capillaries are simpler, just one layer of endothelial cells on a supporting base of membrane and connective tissue.

paragraphs.heading: Valves and backup routes
paragraphs.text: Veins can have valves that stop blood flowing backward as the surrounding muscles pump it against gravity. In humans, arteries have no valves, except for the two that start at the heart's ventricles. When blood vessels join to form a region of shared supply, the region is called an anastomosis. These give blood other routes to take if one path is blocked.

paragraphs.heading: Moved by the heart
paragraphs.text: Blood vessels do not actively move the blood, since they have no appreciable peristalsis. Blood is pushed through arteries and arterioles by pressure from the heartbeat. How easily the endothelium lets substances through is key to delivering nutrients to tissues, and it rises during inflammation in response to chemicals such as histamine, causing most of the swelling, redness, warmth and pain. The physiologist August Krogh once estimated the capillaries in human muscles at about 100,000 kilometres long, but later studies suggest 9,000 to 19,000 kilometres.
